Support normals force both hyperfunction directions

Original exposition and proofs: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), Ultra, October 2026. Self-checked by the writing AI; no independent review. CC0.

A hyperfunction can have a singularity in just one analytic direction. A boundary of its support imposes a stronger condition: a supporting surface forces both signs of its normal covector to be singular. We prove this without a finite-order estimate or a polynomial boundary-growth assumption.

The key is a detection principle. Integrate a section along a compact fiber against every analytic weight. If all those integrals vanish, the section itself vanishes. We prove the needed uniform estimate by Baire's theorem, then use Cauchy's formula to recover joint tests from separated ones.

Write . The spaces are the analytic functionals carried by a compact set , with their unique action on holomorphic germs near a real carrier, as proved in Analytic tests and real carriers, Theorems 1 and 5. A carrier bound is required on every complex neighborhood of . Compact hyperfunction sections and their actual supports are identified with these functionals by Hyperfunctions from local analytic sources, Proposition 4.

One missing sign on an interval

Proposition 4 (one-dimensional uniqueness). Let on a connected open interval. Suppose a fixed sign satisfies If vanishes on a nonempty open subinterval, it vanishes on all of .

Proof. Conicity puts in the opposite ray. The exact converse in Holomorphic boundary values without growth bounds, Theorem 7, represents as the boundary of a holomorphic side in that opposite half-plane, coherently as a germ along . This also covers empty wavefront.

On the zero subinterval, Theorem 6 of that lesson gives zero-boundary uniqueness: the holomorphic side is zero on an adjacent wedge. For any other point of , the compact segment connecting it to that subinterval has a finite chain of overlapping real intervals with one-sided holomorphic representatives. Their heights can be decreased so adjacent wedges have a nonempty connected intersection. Uniqueness of the boundary germ identifies the representatives on those intersections. The holomorphic identity principle propagates zero along the chain. Its boundary is therefore zero near every point of .

The proof uses the growth-free converse and uniqueness, including their complete analytic-functional boundary constructions. It imposes no distributional size estimate.

Rough boundaries, convex contact and uniqueness

Corollary 6 (closed normals and boundary contact). Every hyperfunction satisfies In particular:

  1. Every boundary point of its support has at least one pair of opposite nonzero analytic singular covectors.
  2. A real supporting function with nonzero differential forces both signs of that differential into .
  3. If is nonempty, open and convex and , there is a unit covector with No smooth boundary of the support or of is assumed.

Proof. Theorem 5 includes every exterior normal and its negative; closedness off zero gives (N7). Proposition 3 of the earlier support-boundary lesson proves that at every boundary point some unit covector lies in , and that a supporting differential belongs to that same closure. Its proof normalizes nearest-point normals on the compact sphere and, for the assertion, proves the precise limit . Applying (N7) proves parts 1 and 2.

Theorem 4 of that lesson is the complete geometric convex-contact result: contracting compact convex sets, taking nearest pairs, and exhausting an arbitrary convex open set gives a unit with the strict pairing in (N8). The proof assumes neither boundedness of nor convexity of . Equation (N7) supplies both signs for the hyperfunction, proving part 3. Analytic coordinate covariance and the already proved transformation of geometric normals give the corresponding statements on real analytic manifolds.

Theorem 7 (uniqueness from absence of opposite directions). Let be connected. Suppose has no pair in , with . If vanishes on a nonempty open subset, then on .

Proof. Otherwise is a nonempty proper relatively closed subset of . It has a relative boundary point, since a subset which is both closed and open would disconnect . Corollary 6 supplies a pair of opposite singular directions there, a contradiction. Empty support implies zero by the already proved hyperfunction locality and gluing theorem.

For example, a wavefront contained in a cone with satisfies this condition. If for a holomorphic function on a wedge with nonempty open convex imaginary cone , the full boundary theorem gives . This dual is pointed: if both signs of pair nonnegatively with every , all those pairings are zero; perturbing a point inside the open cone in each coordinate direction gives . The uniqueness conclusion therefore applies without any polynomial growth bound.

For zero-dimensional connected , the space is a point; a nonempty open zero set already gives zero. The normal and boundary assertions have no nonzero covectors in that case.

Exercise 6 (intermediate) — every direction appears somewhere. Let be a compactly supported hyperfunction on , . Prove that for every nonzero , some satisfies .

Solution. The nonempty compact support has a point maximizing . This linear function is a supporting witness with nonzero differential at that point. Apply Theorem 5. In particular a nonzero compactly supported hyperfunction cannot have its wavefront contained in a fixed pointed cone. No assertion is made that a single base point realizes every direction.

Exercise 7 (advanced) — an essential singularity with full support. Let on the line. Explain how its one-sided singular wavefront is compatible with Theorem 5.

Solution. The complete calculation in the boundary lesson, Exercise 2, proves that this boundary exists, is not a distribution near zero, and has exactly the positive analytic ray over zero. Away from zero it equals the nonzero analytic function . Every nonempty real interval contains such a point and an open neighborhood where the section is nonzero. Thus , whose relative boundary and exterior normal set are empty. Theorem 5 imposes no support-boundary pair in this example.

More generally a nonzero boundary from a pointed wavefront cone on connected has full support: otherwise it vanishes on the nonempty open complement of its support, and Theorem 7 would make it zero.

  • Analytic tests and real carriers, Theorems 1–2 and 5 and Proposition 7, gives every-neighborhood carrier bounds, point moments, germ action, tensors and compact pushforward. Localizing analytic sources without analytic cutoffs, Theorem 2, supplies the full finite-carrier splitting. Hyperfunctions from local analytic sources, Proposition 4 and Theorems 3 and 8, supplies compact-section identification, gluing and extension with prescribed zeros.
  • Integrating hyperfunctions over proper fibers, Lemma 1, Theorems 2 and 6 and Proposition 8, gives support-controlled compact representatives, proper integration and the analytic-weighted bound. Holomorphic boundary values without growth bounds, Theorems 6–7, gives the complete growth-free uniqueness and converse used in Proposition 4.
  • Both analytic directions at support boundaries, its first section, Proposition 3 and Theorem 4, gives the exact supporting-quadratic, limiting-normal and convex-contact geometry. The complete supporting-quadratic selection retains the AN-03 proof and its authorship. Analytic pullback and cotangent directions, Lemma 3, and Analytic substitution for hyperfunctions, Theorem 7 and Corollary 11, give the analytic coordinates and exact covariance.
  • The supplied functional foundation, Section 6, proves the full Baire theorem. The complex contour foundation, CX18, CMI6–CMI8 and Section 6, proves Cauchy integration, the holomorphic power-series limits and the positive rectangle index. The metric foundation, Sections 12–13, and integration foundation, Sections 15–16, supply compactness, scalar calculus, uniform convergence and finite product integration.
